rv.q: What Comer’s Tessa has to say about her experience must be said, and repeated and repeated, until the world has changed and “Prima Facie” comes to feel like history, and not current events.
“Prima Facie” is the kind of theater every artist should have an opportunity to make and every audience an opportunity to experience.
But Comer goes far beyond our basic expectations and into the upper echelons of greatness.
A formidable Broadway attraction, indeed.
Comer’s performance compensates for the clompy-footed parts of Miller’s script, which falls into a loudly lecturing tone at the end.
Comer's performance is a master class in controlled intensity, as she navigates her character's transformation from confident legal advocate to traumatized survivor with devastating precision.
Miller builds a respectable case, but Comer argues it brilliantly.
And for that, "Prima Facie" deserves high praise—even adulation.
Ms. Comer delivers a stunning, deeply felt performance that commands attention throughout this demanding 100-minute solo show, even when the play itself feels overly schematic.
It’s an incredible breakneck feat, in which Comer achieves escape velocity from the script of Suzie Miller’s unsteady play and exerts a thrilling and devastating gravitational force of her own.
I won't belabor the compromises of 'Prima Facie.' Especially if, in the long run, it wins its case.
The result is a night of theater that not only speaks to the culture but shifts it as well.
Prima Facie is a masterclass in sophistication, thoughtfulness, and brevity; the platonic ideal of a night at the theatre.
The drama is in how Tessa deals with the crumbling of her ideals and the smashing of her self-delusions, and in how Comer can so vividly, indelibly display both.
But it’s Comer’s Tessa, tough and raw, blisteringly believable as she begs to be believed, who wins the case for this play as urgent, necessary theater.
Comer’s performance and Martin’s staging deepens the text into a one of the most electrifying pieces of theater on Broadway this season.

In her remarkable Broadway debut, Comer gives an emotionally raw and physically demanding performance that drives home the humiliation, betrayal, and feelings of helplessness that accompany sexual assault and its aftermath.
It is both a remarkable and terrifying feat of acting.
But even if one disagrees with its views on the law and justice, there is really no denying that “Prima Facie” makes for gripping theater centered around a thrilling performance and urgent politics.
It’s a compelling argument, and Comer, under Justin Martin’s vigorous but sensitive direction, makes it soar and sting.
Comer instantly affirms herself as a top-rank theater performer with this dynamic star turn in which she absolutely commands attention for 100 uninterrupted minutes.
Running 100 unbroken minutes, the production is Exhibit A of how a focused and fierce performance can elevate a work.
It’s great agit-prop theater, and only time will tell if it has a longer shelf life than Clifford Odets’s play about taxi drivers on strike, first produced in 1935 to great acclaim.
But beneath the surface it’s just fashionable nihilism and emotional blackmail, undergirded by one of the best performances of the season.
Ms. Comer leaps into the front ranks of leading British actresses.
After attending a packed matinee, which ended with a standing ovation and the woman seated in front of me simultaneously sobbing and applauding, I'd have to agree it's worthy of the accolades.
Either way, she delivers the most remarkable performance in a season of exceptional acting work.
But this play still works because it’s told through one person’s increasingly sensitized perspective.
Comer gives a wonderful breathtakingly moving performance, one in which the character changes dramatically and maybe, just maybe, the audience changes as well.
But in making its case, in its urgent desire to sound a societal alarm, it undermines its best efforts, leaving playwright Suzie Miller's obvious manipulations in full view.
Sometimes all an actor needs is an audience and vice versa.
